title: Spencer Egart- Tooling for Roguelikes and Procgen
speaker: Spencer Egart
summary: Spencer Egart, a game engineer on Slime Rancher 2 and procgen hobbyist, argues that developers can build content-creation tools for procedural generation that give a non-code interface to the generation procedure. As a case study he builds a node-graph tool in Unity with the open-source xNode framework for a simple dungeon generator (empty level, binary space partitioning, prefab room placement, A* hallways, player spawn), including a branching node for regions too small for prefabs. He recommends modular, reusable, parameterised steps and a friendly UI, points to existing tools (Dungeon Architect, xNode, Sxelix-style procedural engine), and in Q&A discusses weighing time saved against time invested, especially in jams like 7DRL.

insights.claim: Procedural generators can be exposed through content-creation tools that give a non-code interface to the generation procedure, usable by non-engineers and teams as well as the developer.
insights.detail: Egart frames tools as software that creates content by creating the procedures of procgen. He caveats 'non-code': visual scripting and domain-specific languages are in a way still code; he means not writing code in an IDE.
insights.quote: you can build and use tools for your roguelike for procgen for uh your team for yourself for non-engineers

insights.claim: A basic dungeon generator can be built in four steps: start with an empty area, split it with binary space partitioning, fill regions with prefab rooms, and connect them with A* hallways.
insights.detail: BSP repeatedly halves the space into rectangles. Egart's example used only two prefab room shapes. He uses A* pathfinding for hallways because it makes it easy for corridors to skirt the edges of other rooms.
insights.quote: you use binary space partitioning which if you're not familiar is a way of just taking a space and splitting it in half repeatedly

insights.claim: Egart built his dungeon generator as a visual node graph in Unity with the open-source xNode framework, getting the drag-and-drop UI working in a couple of hours.
insights.detail: The graph runs left to right: blank level, BSP, prefab rooms, A* hallways, then a node placing the player spawn, showing that non-geometry steps can be part of the same pipeline.
insights.quote: a tool that i built in unity using a framework called xnode which is a an open source library for unity

insights.claim: Node pipelines can branch with if-then-else nodes, such as routing BSP regions too small for prefab rooms into a node that carves plain square rooms instead.
insights.detail: A 'region has room' node sends regions with a prefab room out one output and empty ones out another; empty regions get a padded rectangle carved, then everything feeds back into the A* hallway carver. Real generators will have more steps and branching.
insights.quote: that allows us to branch in a kind of if then else manner

insights.claim: The same step-by-step node approach used for dungeon geometry can place encounters and loot or generate items, for example by piping through base item and curse nodes.
insights.detail: Egart says any problem whose component steps can be identified can be broken into nodes, layers in a list, or another useful representation.
insights.quote: i could also be placing enemy encounters in here i could be using this tool to place a loot i could be using it to generate loot

insights.claim: Procgen tools should be built from modular, self-contained, reusable steps with exposed parameters, because more interconnectable pieces give the tool more expressive power.
insights.detail: Egart likens steps to Lego pieces. His BSP node exposes parameters like minimum and maximum region size, adding power to each step.
insights.quote: the more reusable and interconnectable your lego pieces are the more expressive power you're going to eventually have with that tool

insights.claim: The secretly hard part of procgen tooling is making it friendly to use, so frameworks that handle the UI free you to focus on the generation itself.
insights.detail: Egart points to existing tools: Dungeon Architect (Unity and Unreal, based on the cyclic generation from Unexplored's developers), xNode, and a procedural engine for Unity that generates trees and buildings in a similar way.
insights.quote: the secretly hard part of all of this is making it uh friendly to work with

insights.claim: Decide whether to build a tool by weighing time saved against time invested, and generally avoid building tools during a game jam like 7DRL.
insights.detail: Egart's demo generator sits in a project named '7DRL 2021', and he shipped no game for that jam. On Slime Rancher he asks whether a tool will save everyone a lot of time. When a tool is for broader expressive range, the value is harder to quantify and becomes a judgment call.
insights.quote: you can make a very um kind of mathematical judgment of time saved versus time invested
